card.name: Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra Dance
card.tagline: Salatiga dance depicting Mangkunegara I's elite concubine archer regiment.
card.profile: Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra is a classical Javanese dance originating from the city of Salatiga in Central Java, Indonesia. It commemorates the female warrior regiment of garwa ampil (concubines) belonging to Mangkunegara I (Raden Mas Said), who displayed their military discipline during the Treaty of Salatiga on 17 March 1757. Classified as a flexible presentation, it can be executed as a solo, in pairs, or in larger formations. The choreography merges the court traditions of the Surakarta style with grassroots Prajuritan folk martial dances.
card.insight: Marking the 17 March 1757 Treaty of Salatiga, this dance depicts the Jurit Ampil, an elite unit of armed concubines fielded by Prince Mangkunegara I brandishing bows, arrows, and daggers.

card.profile_long:
Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra, or Beksan Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra, is a classical dance form created in Salatiga, Central Java Province, Indonesia. The dance serves as a living historical portrait of military power and courtly hierarchy in eighteenth-century Java, specifically celebrating the martial concubines of Raden Mas Said, renowned as Mangkunegara I or Pangeran Samber Nyawa. In Javanese, 'jurit' signifies soldier, 'garwa ampil' denotes the concubines of the royal house of Mangkunegaran, and 'warastra' specifies the bow and arrow. Together, the dance's title and structure evoke the armed female contingent that was famously paraded during the historic negotiations of the Salatiga Treaty on 17 March 1757.

The historical background reflects a critical turning point in Javanese history. The Treaty of Salatiga brought together three powerful leaders: Sultan Hamengkubuwana I of Yogyakarta, Sunan Pakubuwana III of Surakarta, and Mangkunegara I. During this assembly, each sovereign displayed his military might through various bregada, or armed ceremonial units. Mangkunegara I chose to demonstrate his distinctive Jurit Ampil, a regiment formed entirely of his garwa ampil who had been trained as disciplined combatants. The choreography recreates this imposing court spectacle by embodying both military severity and royal grace.

Choreographically, Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra is categorized as a free-style dance that offers versatile performance options: it may be staged by a solitary dancer, executed in balanced pairs, or presented as a synchronized group. The movement foundation bridges two distinct worlds of Javanese movement arts. It synthesizes the refined, codified aesthetic of classical Surakarta-style dance (gaya Surakarta) with the earthy vigor of Prajuritan folk dance, borrowing numerous martial stances and weapon drills directly from the latter tradition. While grounded in classical movement rules, the dance incorporates modern performance staging to appeal to contemporary audiences.

Musical accompaniment is provided by a traditional Javanese gamelan ensemble tuned to the pelog scale. The orchestration utilizes specific core instruments, including the gender, kendhang (double-headed barrel drum), demung, saron, kenong, kempul, and large gong. The musical structure shifts through traditional Javanese compositional forms, transitioning between lancaran, srepeg, and palaran structures to mirror the dramatic intensity of troop maneuvers and weapon demonstrations.

The dancers are outfitted in distinctive female warrior attire that conveys military authority and royal elegance. Their hair is bound into a compact small bun topped with an ornate golden crown. The primary garment is a short-sleeved blue shirt accented with gold embellishments, secured around the waist by a belt and paired with a traditional wrapped dodot cloth over knee-length trousers. Essential to the dancer's persona is an array of classical weaponry: the jemparing (bow and arrow), endhong (quiver), nyenyep (arrows), gendewa (bow), and the cundrik (a short traditional dagger). Staged makeup is deliberately applied to sharpen facial lines and project the resolute character of an armed palace guard.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance commemorates a pivotal historical event in Central Java: the Treaty of Salatiga, enacted on 17 March 1757. During the assembly to finalize the treaty, three rulers—Hamengkubuwana I, Pakubuwana III, and Mangkunegara I (Raden Mas Said, also known as Pangeran Samber Nyawa)—exhibited their military strength. Mangkunegara I showcased multiple bregada (military units), among which was the Jurit Ampil, a unit composed exclusively of his garwa ampil (concubines) trained as soldiers. The dance translates this historical display into a formal classical composition created in the city of Salatiga.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra is classified as a free-style dance, meaning it can be performed in groups, pairs, or solo. It synthesizes classical Surakarta-style court dance with regional folk dance forms, borrowing extensively from the Prajuritan martial dance tradition. Dancers manipulate traditional weaponry including bows and daggers while maintaining classical postures blended with military precision. Modern staging elements have also been introduced to adapt the choreography to modern performance contexts.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by a Javanese gamelan ensemble playing in the pelog scale. The instrumental layout includes the gender, kendhang, demung, saron, kenong, kempul, and gong. The musical compositions used to drive the performance and punctuate the choreography incorporate standard Javanese musical forms, specifically lancaran, srepeg, and palaran structures.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear female warrior attire. The hair is gathered in a small bun adorned with a golden crown. The core costume features a short-sleeved blue shirt embellished with gold trim, a belt, and a dodot wrapped over knee-length trousers. The weaponry kit includes the jemparing (bow and arrow set), composed of the gendewa (bow), nyenyep (arrow), and endhong (quiver), alongside a cundrik (dagger). Theatrical makeup is applied specifically to accentuate the bold expression and disciplined character of a royal soldier.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The choreography conveys the complex concepts embedded in its title: 'jurit' (soldier), 'garwa ampil' (concubine of Mangkunegara I), and 'warastra' (bow and arrow). It stands as a representation of female military discipline and royal sovereignty, reflecting on the historical unity and territorial negotiations established during the Salatiga Treaty of 1757.
sections.notable_figures: The central historical figure is Raden Mas Said, titularly known as Mangkunegara I and famously referred to as Pangeran Samber Nyawa, who formed and commanded the original Jurit Ampil concubine troops.
sections.regional_variants: The dance originates in the city of Salatiga in Central Java, drawing choreographic material from both the court styles of Surakarta and local Prajuritan folk martial dancing.
sections.lineage: Beksan Jurit Ampil Kridha Warastra descends genealogically from the martial traditions of the Mangkunegaran court, merging Surakarta-style Javanese classical dance with vernacular Prajuritan soldier dances.

basic_steps: Assume a balanced warrior stance carrying the gendewa (bow) and cundrik (dagger).
Execute Prajuritan-derived martial footwork blended with Surakarta classical body alignment.
Draw the nyenyep (arrow) from the endhong (quiver) and nock to the gendewa.
Manoeuvre through floor pathways transitioning between lancaran and srepeg musical structures.
teaching.rhythm: Pelog gamelan structures featuring lancaran, srepeg, and palaran meters
teaching.formation: Solo, pairs, or group bregada line formations
teaching.level_notes: Requires coordination of handheld traditional weaponry (bow, arrows, dagger) with Javanese classical and folk movement registers.

music_profile.sound_description: A Javanese gamelan ensemble playing in the pelog scale, marked by the resonant punctuations of the gong, kempul, and kenong, balanced by the rhythmic drive of the kendhang barrel drum and melodic metallophones including the gender, demung, and saron, shifting through lancaran, srepeg, and palaran sections.

movement_profile.posture: Disciplined female warrior posture blending refined Surakarta-style court alignment with grounded Prajuritan martial readiness.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Armed hand gestures handling the jemparing (bow and arrow) and unsheathing or brandishing the cundrik dagger.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Controlled torso and hip carriage wrapped in a dodot and belt over knee-length trousers.

movement_profile.tempo_feel: Shifts dynamically between the steady cadence of lancaran, the urgent momentum of srepeg, and the lyrical tension of palaran.
